extracted.intended_audience: media studies students, writers, teachers, and narrative analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Using Roland Barthes' five narrative codes to analyse or construct media texts by labelling units of discourse (lexias) with hermeneutic, proairetic, semantic, symbolic, and cultural codes to reveal plot mechanics and connotative depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermeneutic Codes (enigma codes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a writer deliberately withholds information from the audience to leave a plot point unexplained, they are using a hermeneutic code. More commonly known as enigma codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'snares' and 'partial answers' to delay resolution and keep engagement; leave questions open that prompt the audience to form interpretations. Frequently used in mystery and horror (examples: Scream (1996), Get Out (2017)). In Barthes' example, the unusual title 'Sarrasine' acts as a hermeneutic code because it forces the reader to question its meaning until revealed later. Anti-pattern: revealing the answer too early removes the enigma's function; conversely, never resolving an enigma can frustrate audiences unless that frustration is intentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proairetic Codes (action/plot-beat codes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proairetic codes are plot points which are caused by previous events and lead to other actions (the sequencing of events into a coherent order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label obvious cause→effect beats (car chases, climactic battles, quest steps, product-use transformations) as proairetic. These create temporal tension by making the audience wonder about the outcome (e.g., will the criminal be caught? will the hero win?). Examples: Captain America: Civil War fight sequence; Frozen 2 quest events (wrecked ship, map, awakening spirits). Anti-pattern: disconnected or non-causal events that break story logic weaken the proairetic chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic Codes (connotative signifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some codes have 'flickers of meaning'—signs that carry connotations beyond their basic definition and give more insight into characters, setting and plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify objects, costumes, locations, or repeated details that connote traits or contexts (e.g., James Bond's tuxedos → sophistication; Wayne Manor → wealth; Platform 9 ¾ → entry into magic). In films this includes establishing shots which connotatively position characters (e.g., establishing shot of Wayne Manor connotes Bruce Wayne's wealth). Semantic codes function at the level of connotation without necessarily invoking binary opposition. Use them to enrich characterisation and worldbuilding. Anti-pattern: treating every detail as purely denotative misses potential semantic layering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic Codes (thematic/structural devices/binaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic codes are best defined as thematic or structural devices—Barthes suggested they are a 'battle' between contrasting signs; binary opposites and deliberate antithesis elevate signs into symbolic codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for contrasts and juxtapositions that produce thematic meaning (hot/cold, personal/collective). Examples: lightsaber colours in Star Wars (Jedi vs Sith); the juxtaposition of the Dawn of Man bone and a spaceship in 2001: A Space Odyssey to connect evolution and technology. Recurring signs whose interpreted meaning shifts across the text can become symbolic. Note: symbolic and semantic codes overlap (both connotative), but symbolic codes are characterised by antithesis and structural comparison. Use symbolic codes to trace thematic oppositions and long-term structural patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural Codes (intertextual/social knowledge references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural codes are allusions to concepts and ideas that exist outside the text; they rely on the audience's framework of knowledge to be fully decoded (historical, social, psychological, literary references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify references, homages, and social signs that presuppose shared knowledge (e.g., The Big Bang Theory's Star Trek/Star Wars references; The Simpsons' homage to 2001). Cultural codes include intertextuality and social conventions (e.g., formal coronation clothing connoting royal status). Use cultural codes to connect the text to wider cultural discourses; be aware that their effectiveness depends on audience familiarity. Anti-pattern: relying on obscure cultural references that your target audience cannot decode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexias (units of analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Barthes divided the text into units of reading, or lexias. A lexia might include a few words or several sentences, and they can all be labelled with his five codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the five codes, segment the text into lexias as analyzable units—each lexia can be examined for hermeneutic, proairetic, semantic, symbolic, and cultural functions. Lexias help operationalise Barthes' method for both short excerpts and longer media texts. Practical tip: select lexia boundaries where a shift in signification or action occurs. Anti-pattern: using arbitrarily large lexias that conflate multiple functions and obscure which code applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional grouping of the five codes (chronology vs connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Barthes grouped the five codes by function: the hermeneutic and proairetic codes provide the internal chronology of the narrative, while the semantic, symbolic and cultural codes work on a connotative level and add depth to the tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or constructing narrative, treat hermeneutic/proairetic codes as governing sequence, mystery, and causal action; treat semantic/symbolic/cultural codes as layers of meaning, theme, and intertextual resonance. This division helps analysts separate plot mechanics from connotative depth. Use it to ensure both narrative drive (chronology) and thematic richness (connotation) are addressed. Anti-pattern: focusing solely on plot sequencing without attending to connotative coding, or vice versa, results in flat or aimless storytelling.
